When inferring causal effects from observational studies, one of the assumptions that's generally required is the exchangeability assumption. My question is, why is this assumption called the "exchangeability" assumption when it's a statement about independence? But what is the relationship between exchangeability and independence in the causal inference context? > My question is, why is this assumption called the "exchangeability" assumption when it's a statement about independence? If you made treatment and outcome independent by adjusting for the appropriate variables $Z$ (check backdoor criterion, for example), you can also see this as *conditional exchangeability*, e.g., $Y^a \perp\!\!\!\perp A \mid Z $. $\begingroup$ So exchangeability here is not referring to the probabilistic definition, i.e., that a sequence of random variables is exchangeable if permuting them in another order does not change the joint distribution, but rather that you can interchange the treated and control groups without changing the outcomes, correct?

Any node with an edge to at least two other nodes must be drawn on the graph. 2. **Path.** A path is a sequence of edges connecting two nodes. 3. **Collider along a path.** A node such as \(B\) where to directed edges collide: \(A\rightarrow B \leftarrow C\). A collider blocks the path. * \(A\) and \(B\) are *marginally dependent* if and only if there exists an unblocked path connecting them. * \(A\) and \(B\) are *marginally independent* if and only if any paths connecting them are blocked. ## 4.2 Conditional independence. **Slides.** After class, read Hernán and Robins 2020 Chapter 6.3 and 6.4, and especially Fine Point 6.1 of which this page is an abbreviation. Often, we want to condition on some set of variables \(\vec{L}\) so that conditional exchangeability holds. A path is blocked if any node on the path is blocked. If every node on a path is open, then the entire path is open. 1. A non-collider is blocked if is conditioned on, otherwise it is open. 2. A collider is open if it or any of its descendants are conditioned on. ## 4.3 Lab: DAGs Review and Causal discovery. **Slides.** After class, read Hernán and Robins 2020 Fine Point 6.3. In this lab, we’re reviewing some DAG basics such as identifying paths and determining whether a path is open or closed. We’ll also talk a bit about causal discovery and practice creating DAGs from data. ## 4.4 Sufficient adjustment sets. **Slides.** After class, read Hernán and Robins 2020 7.1–7.4. When marginal exchangeability does not hold, we may be able to condition on some set of variables \(\vec{L}\) so that conditional exchangeability holds. We can accomplish this by blocking all non-causal paths between \(A\) and \(Y\). A set that does that is called a sufficient adjustment set. To find a sufficient adjustment set, we will use the backdoor criterion:. 1. The set \(L\) blocks all backdoor paths. 2. The set \(L\) does not contain any descendants of \(A\).

How is it allowed to say that an ordinary differential equation with initial condition has no solution? What is a closed form solution for a differential equation? A closed-form solution of an ordinary differential equation (ODE) is an explicit formula that expresses the dependent variable(s) as elementary or well-defined special functions of the independent variable and of arbitrary constants. In the context of an initial value problem (IVP), a closed-form solution gives the exact state at any time directly in terms of the initial conditions. A closed-form solution of an ordinary differential equation (ODE) is an explicit formula that expresses the dependent variable(s) as elementary or well-defined special functions of the independent variable and of arbitrary constants. In the context of an initial value problem (IVP), a closed-form solution gives the exact state at any time directly in terms of the initial conditions. * Exact solution: a closed-form expression y(t; t0,y0) that satisfies both the differential equation and the initial condition for all t in its domain. - When integrals or characteristic equations lead to special functions (Airy, Bessel, hypergeometric), the closed form will include those; initial conditions pick the linear combination of basis solutions. Why closed-form gives the exact solution relative to initial conditions. * Sensitivity and conditioning: closed forms make it possible to compute exact derivatives of the solution with respect to initial conditions and parameters (variational equations), used in adjoint methods and parameter estimation. This encapsulates what a closed-form solution is, how initial conditions are used to fix arbitrary constants to produce the exact solution, and why such solutions are central in numerical analysis for verification, error analysis, and guiding solver choice.
